idiom_name: mutableMapOf per scope plus a parent link (ArrayDeque for the scope stack), sealed Symbol hierarchy
implementation_notes: Kotlin's collections make the table terse - mutableMapOf<String, Symbol>() per scope with putIfAbsent for duplicate detection, a nullable Scope parent link (or ArrayDeque<Scope> as the open-scope stack), and a sealed interface Symbol with data-class subtypes for the entry kinds - but the structure itself is still written by hand: define inserts into the innermost map, lookup walks outward, and the define/resolve phases are yours. What replaces the classic structure is mutableMapOf/ArrayDeque plus Kotlin's null-safety (a nullable parent terminates the chain); Kotlin's own front end solves the same problem internally with FIR symbol providers, scopes and phase-ordered resolution (FirResolvePhase), but none of that is exposed as a reusable library. Keep the hand-written form for your language or DSL; when analysing Kotlin itself the supported route is the Analysis API over PSI, not a public symbol table.
pitfalls: mutableMapOf returns a LinkedHashMap that is not thread-safe: a resolver shared between coroutines or threads needs confinement, a mutex, or an immutable snapshot (toMap()) once the pass ends.
val protects the reference, not the map: publishing a scope after resolution lets later phases mutate it, so convert to read-only maps when the pass finishes.
Null-safety hides absence: symbols[name] returns null both for 'not declared here' and for a stored null value, so never model symbols as nullable inside the map.
